finding: Most songs visit the chart briefly while a handful stay almost the whole time.
evidence: Median 7 days on the chart, mean 29.4. The longest stay is Something in the Orange by Zach Bryan: 536 of 555 snapshot days.
caveat: Days are counted on snapshot days. The 50 songs that were on the chart on the first day and the 50 that were still there on the last day are cut off by the window of the file.

finding: About a third of the places belong to new songs, and many places belong to songs that have been there for months.
evidence: After the warm-up, songs younger than 30 days fill about 17 of the 50 places, songs older than 90 days about 21 and songs older than 180 days about 11.
caveat: In the first weeks of the file the age of a song is understated (a song that was already on the chart on day one looks new).

finding: The top of the chart is stable and the bottom churns.
evidence: Position 1 was held by 54 different songs in the whole file, position 50 by 232. A song at number one is still at number one the next day 84% of the time, at number 50 only 20%.
caveat: The rates come from 27,700 song-days that have a following snapshot.

finding: Songs move more the further down the chart they sit.
evidence: In the top 10 a song keeps exactly the same position on 55% of days, in positions 21-50 on 23%. The average daily move grows from 0.3 places at number 1 to 4.3 at number 50.
caveat: Measured over the song-days that have a previous day.

finding: Runs begin and end at the bottom of the chart; leaving from the top 20 is rare.
evidence: 57% of the 1,931 runs that began inside the file start in positions 41-50 and 69% end there. Only 4% (79 runs) end in the top 20.
caveat: First-time entries can start high (25% begin in the top 10); songs that come back almost never do.

finding: New entries cluster at the start of the week.
evidence: 67% of first-time entries and 46% of all entries fall on a Monday or a Tuesday. On an average day 3.5 of the 50 places change hands.
caveat: The weekdays are those recorded in the file. Its calendar appears to run about a year ahead of real release dates, so this is a pattern of the file and not a statement about real release days.

finding: Big one-week climbs exist but are rare, and most fades are gradual.
evidence: The fastest riser, i like the way you kiss me by Artemas, gained 43 places in a week (from 46 to 3). The 119 gradual fades lose a median of 3.4 places a week.
caveat: 79 more complete runs left the chart from the top 20; they were removed, not faded, and are not counted as fades. 3 of the ten fastest risers look like holiday songs by their titles.

finding: A run that starts higher lasts longer.
evidence: Complete runs that start in the top 10 last a median of 12.5 days, runs that start in 41-50 last 3. Spearman correlation of entry position and run length: -0.36.
caveat: Only the 1,881 complete runs are used. The sign is negative because position 1 is the best. Descriptive; Phase 5 tests it.

finding: A small number of songs earn most of the chart points.
evidence: 52 songs (5.5% of 944) earn half of all chart points and the biggest 100 earn 68%. Gini coefficient across songs: 0.78.
caveat: Chart points are 51 minus the position, added up over every day a song is on the chart.

finding: The songs that last carry the chart; the songs that only visit hardly count.
evidence: 123 songs (13%) that stayed 61 days or more hold 72% of the points. The 313 songs that stayed one to three days hold 1.4%.
caveat: The classes are defined by days on the chart, and the days also drive the chart points, so the link between class and points is partly built in.

finding: High popularity is not one artist's property, and singles are over-represented among the most popular songs.
evidence: The 15 songs with the highest average popularity come from 15 different artists; 73% of them are singles, against 23% of all songs.
caveat: Only songs with at least 14 days of scores are ranked (335 songs). 189 chart rows with a score of 0 were treated as missing in Phase 2.

finding: A higher peak goes with a longer stay.
evidence: Songs that reached number one (54 songs) stayed a median of 99.5 days; the 638 songs that never reached the top 10 stayed a median of 4. Spearman correlation of best position and days on the chart: -0.59.
caveat: Partly built in: a longer stay gives a song more chances to reach a high peak. This is a pattern, not proof that a high peak causes a long stay.

finding: Many artists share the chart, but very unevenly.
evidence: HHI 254 on a scale that ends at 10,000, effective number of artists 39.3 out of 243, Gini 0.78. Taylor Swift holds 7.5% of the chart points, Zach Bryan 6.7%, and the ten biggest artists 41%.
caveat: Artists are counted by the first-named artist of each song, so a featured guest has no points of their own.

finding: Most artists place a single song, but the artists with many songs hold most of the points.
evidence: 142 of the 243 artists (58%) placed exactly one song and together hold 16% of the points; the 36 artists with five or more songs hold 64%.
caveat: First-named artist only.

finding: The artist who leads the chart changes from month to month, and some months are far more shared than others.
evidence: 14 different artists led in at least one of the 19 months. The biggest monthly share was 23.6% (Taylor Swift, April 2025). The effective number of artists ran from 11.1 (September 2024) to 37.1 (December 2024).
caveat: The first and last months of the file are part months.

finding: There are two routes to a big share of the chart: many songs (breadth) or a few songs that last (depth).
evidence: Morgan Wallen placed 10 songs that stayed 167 days each on average; Taylor Swift placed 96 songs at 21 days each, against a chart average of 29. Across the 63 artists with at least three songs, songs placed and days per song have a Spearman correlation of -0.23.
caveat: Descriptive; the correlation is moderate and only covers artists with at least three songs.

finding: Number one and the top 10 are shared by many artists, led by a few.
evidence: 37 artists held number one. Sabrina Carpenter held it for 66 days, and the top five holders account for 41% of the number-one days. The top 10 had 5,550 song-days from 93 artists; the ten biggest of them hold 44%.
caveat: First-named artist only.

finding: Popularity and chart position are only loosely related.
evidence: Spearman correlation 0.25 across song-days, 0.16 across songs and 0.21 within songs (335 songs with at least 14 days).
caveat: A score of 0 was treated as missing in Phase 2 (189 rows were repaired from the same song's other days).

finding: Top-10 song-days score higher and more unevenly than the rest.
evidence: Median popularity 93 in the top 10, 89 in positions 11-20 and 88 in 21-50. 38% of top-10 song-days score 95 or more, against 14% and 9%. Kruskal-Wallis H = 1,635.
caveat: A song appears on many days, so song-days are not independent; the formal comparison in Phase 5 has to allow for that.

finding: The average popularity of the chart slipped over the period, partly because of the mix of arriving songs.
evidence: The 28-day average fell from 89.4 to 86.2; for songs more than a week into their stay it fell from 90.9 to 89.0.
caveat: Single-day dips are release days: on 17 Aug 2025 15 new songs with an average score of 41, 14 of them from one release by Post Malone, pulled the day's average down to 72.

finding: Songs whose popularity swings more also swing more on the chart, but the link is modest.
evidence: Spearman correlation 0.29 across 335 songs with at least 14 days. Median position swing: 7.2 places in the steadiest fifth of songs, 11.1 in the least steady fifth.
caveat: Songs with fewer than 14 days are left out because a standard deviation over a few days is noisy.

finding: A high first-day score goes with a longer run only when runs that started in the same place are compared.
evidence: Spearman correlation 0.03 over all 1,713 runs, and between 0.14 and 0.49 inside the five starting bands.
caveat: 168 complete runs were left out because their first-day score was a repaired zero. A model that uses first-day popularity must not use repaired values.

finding: Volatility lives in the middle of the chart, not at the ends.
evidence: Median Rank Volatility Index: 5.4 for songs that average the top 10, 12.2 for songs that average 21-30 and 4.4 for 41-50 (493 songs with at least 7 days).
caveat: A song at the very top or the very bottom has little room to move, so part of the pattern is built in.

finding: The explicit share of the chart changed a lot from month to month.
evidence: 48% of song-days overall; by month from 32% (December 2024) to 64% (February 2025), above half in 7 of 19 months.
caveat: The first and last months of the file are part months.

finding: Singles stay about twice as long as album tracks but do not reach the top 10 more often.
evidence: Median stay 13 days for 216 singles against 6 for 728 album tracks; 31% of singles and 33% of album tracks reached the top 10.
caveat: Descriptive; Phase 5 tests the difference. The compilation songs count as album tracks.

finding: Explicit songs reach the top 10 more often but do not stay longer.
evidence: 36% of the 495 explicit songs reached the top 10 against 29% of the 449 others; the median stay is 7 days against 7.
caveat: Descriptive; Phase 5 tests the difference.

finding: Collaborations reach the top 10 a little less often than solo songs.
evidence: 29% of the 122 collaborations against 33% of the 822 solo songs; average popularity is almost the same (80.4 against 79.0).
caveat: A small difference between groups of very different size; Phase 5 tests it.

finding: Longer songs reach the top 10 more often but do not stay longer.
evidence: Share of songs that reached the top 10: 24% under 2:30, then 30%, 32%, 36% and 36% at 4:00 and up. Median days on the chart: 7, 8, 7, 7 and 6.
caveat: Descriptive; Phase 5 tests whether the rise is more than chance.

finding: Albums of 8 to 40 tracks supply most of the chart points, and one-track releases stay longest.
evidence: Albums of 8-15 and 16-40 tracks supply 76% of the songs and 70% of the chart points. One-track releases supply 18% of the songs and 22% of the points and stay a median of 17 days (albums of 16-40 tracks: 6).
caveat: 2 size bands have fewer than 20 songs, so their medians are not reliable. Spearman correlation of tracks on the release and days on the chart: -0.16.

finding: Explicit songs stay longer only among singles.
evidence: Median days on the chart: explicit singles 16.5 against 10 for other singles; explicit album tracks 6 against 7 for other album tracks.
caveat: There are only 104 and 112 songs in the two single groups, so their medians move with a few songs. Phase 5 tests the interaction.

finding: No song attribute is strongly related to any chart outcome.
evidence: The largest correlation between an attribute and an outcome is 0.23 (tracks on the release and average popularity). 25 of the 30 cells are below 0.15 in absolute size.
caveat: A rank correlation sees one-way links only, and three pairs of outcomes (peak and average position, days and average popularity, peak position and rank volatility) are partly built into the measures.
